problems.title: Three intensities
problems.statement: All arrays are FP32 and nothing is cached: every array element is read or written once from DRAM.

parts.prompt: Vector add, c = a + b: FLOP per byte?
Dot product, s = Σ xᵢyᵢ (ignore the single output)?

hints: Count FLOPs per element and bytes per element.
SAXPY: a multiply and an add; reads x and y, writes y.
problems.solution: (a) 1 FLOP / 12 bytes = 0.083. (b) 2 / 12 = 0.167. (c) 2 / 8 = 0.25. All three are far left of any GPU's ridge: memory-bound, and their only goal is full bandwidth.

problems.title: How good is 1.9 ms?
problems.statement: SAXPY over $n = 2^{26}$ floats takes 1.9 ms on the GW-1.

parts.prompt: Lower bound on the time, in ms?
Achieved fraction of peak bandwidth, in %?

problems.solution: (a) $12 \times 2^{26} = 805,306,368$ bytes. (b) $/512\,\text{GB/s} = 1.573$ ms. (c) $82.8\%$: good (80–90% is the practical ceiling), so little is left on the table.

problems.title: Matrix–vector
problems.statement: $y = Ax$ with $A$ an 8192 × 8192 FP32 matrix, read once; x read once, y written once.

parts.prompt: Lower bound on time on the GW-1, in ms?

problems.solution: (a) $2MN / (4MN + 4M + 4N) \approx 0.4999$: essentially 0.5, because each element of A is used once. (b) $\approx 268$ MB at 512 GB/s: 0.524 ms. GEMV is memory-bound on every GPU ever made; GEMM is not (Part 4).

problems.title: Precision moves you on the roofline
problems.statement: Vector add on the GW-1, in different precisions. FP16 math runs at the FP32 rate here; FP64 at 1/32 of it.
problems.solution: (a) $1/6$, (b) $512/6 = 85.3$: half the bytes, twice the speed. (c) $\min(48, 512/24 = 21.3) = 21.3$: even with a 32× slower FP64 unit, vector add is still memory-bound.

problems.title: Fusion on the roofline
problems.statement: Three kernels over n floats: c = a + b, then d = s·c, then e = d + a. Or one fused kernel computing e directly.
hints: Kernel 1: read 2, write 1. Kernel 2: read 1, write 1. Kernel 3: read 2, write 1.
Fused: read a and b, write e.
problems.solution: (a) $12 + 8 + 12 = 32$. (b) 12. (c) 3 FLOPs / 12 bytes = 0.25 (up from 3/32). (d) $32/12 = 2.67\times$: fusion is the single biggest lever for chains of memory-bound operations, and the reason ML compilers exist.

problems.title: The next generation
problems.statement: A new GPU has 4× the GW-1's peak compute and 2× its bandwidth.

parts.prompt: A kernel at I = 4: speedup over the GW-1?

hints: Attainable on each machine, then the ratio.
problems.solution: (a) $6144/1024 = 6$. (b) GW-1: $\min(1536, 2048) = 1536$ (compute-bound); new: $\min(6144, 4096) = 4096$ (now memory-bound): 2.67×. (c) Memory-bound on both: 2×, the bandwidth ratio. As ridges move right, kernels that were compute-bound become memory-bound.

problems.title: A blur's true intensity
problems.statement: A 5-tap horizontal box blur: per output pixel, 4 adds and 1 multiply (by 1/5). FP32 image of 4096 × 4096.

parts.prompt: Intensity counting the source's reads (5 reads, 1 write per pixel)?
Intensity if the cache serves all repeated reads (DRAM sees 1 read, 1 write)?
Lower bound on time in the second case, in ms?

problems.solution: (a) $5/24 = 0.21$. (b) $5/8 = 0.625$. (c) $8 \times 4096^2 / 512\,\text{GB/s} = 0.262$ ms. Intensity is about DRAM traffic, so caching changes it by 3×; both are still memory-bound.

problems.title: Under both roofs
problems.statement: A kernel reaches 30% of peak bandwidth and 2% of peak compute. The profiler shows 12% occupancy and long stalls waiting on memory.

options: Latency: too few requests in flight
More parallelism or more independent loads per thread

problems.solution: It sits well below both roofs, with low occupancy and memory stalls: latency-bound (Part 0's Little's law). More warps, or more loads in flight per warp (Volkov), raise it toward the bandwidth roof; only then do byte-saving optimisations pay.

problems.title: More roofs
problems.statement: The GW-1's tensor cores give 8× the FP32 peak (12,288 GFLOP/s), and its L2 delivers 1,024 GB/s. A GEMM kernel has intensity 16 FLOP/byte against DRAM and 4 FLOP/byte against L2.

parts.prompt: Ridge point of the tensor roof against DRAM?

hints: Attainable = min over all roofs: peak, I_DRAM × B_DRAM, I_L2 × B_L2.
problems.solution: (a) $12288/512 = 24$. (b) $\min(12288, 8192, 4096) = 4096$. (c) L2: the kernel reuses data well from DRAM's point of view but re-reads it from L2 too often. The fix is more reuse in shared memory and registers (Part 4), which raises the L2 intensity.
